claims.text: The alloy is equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi.
Forty hours of high-energy planetary ball milling followed by SPS is an established processing route for equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi.
The reference SPS process uses 1400 °C for 10 minutes under 30 MPa.
SPS at 1300 °C for 10 minutes under 30 MPa after 40 hours of milling will produce grains smaller than 50 nm.
The proposed process will produce a dual-phase BCC/BCC solid-solution structure.
Keeping oxygen below 0.5 wt% suppresses oxide precipitation.
Sintering between 1250 °C and 1350 °C inhibits TiO nucleation and growth.
Solute drag and grain-boundary pinning stabilize the nanocrystalline BCC matrix.
The absence of TiO prevents formation of brittle intermetallic networks and associated embrittlement.
Hall–Petch grain refinement and multi-principal-element solid-solution strengthening jointly increase yield strength.
Nanocrystalline grain size enhances yield strength without the ductility loss typical of coarse-grained brittle alloys.
The proposed material will have a yield strength exceeding 2500 MPa.
The proposed material will have a yield strength higher than the 2709 MPa reference sample.
The reference NbMoTaWVTi sample has a compressive yield strength of 2709 MPa.
The proposed material will have a compressive fracture strain greater than 10%.
The proposed microstructure will be single-phase BCC or contain only a very minor BCC2 phase.
The 1400 °C reference sample has a 1.35 micrometer grain size, 16.1 vol.% TiO, and 11.4% fracture strain.
TiO precipitation becomes dominant above 1380 °C.
Oxygen contents above 0.6 wt% nucleate TiO even at lower sintering temperatures.
TiO formation at the stated temperature or oxygen limits causes brittle fracture and loss of ductility.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires a dual-phase BCC/BCC structure, whereas the predicted outcome specifies a single-phase BCC solid solution or only a very minor BCC2 phase.
A yield-strength criterion of merely greater than 2500 MPa does not establish the accompanying claim that strength is higher than the 2709 MPa baseline.
TiO is alternately described as an oxide, an FCC phase, and a brittle intermetallic. Calling TiO an intermetallic is chemically inconsistent with its identification as an oxide.
The boundary gives precise critical limits of 1380 °C and 0.6 wt% oxygen, while the uncertainty field concedes that the phase-stability limits are not defined by the evidence.
